Imagine waking up to a world forever changed—where uncertainty fills the air, and hope seems just out of reach. Now, picture a small town perched on the edge of North America, suddenly becoming a safe haven for thousands of strangers from distant places. That's the heart of the story we're about to explore together.
In his remarkable book, The Day the World Came to Town: 9/11 in Gander, Newfoundland, Jim DeFede takes us inside this moment when the unimaginable happened. While the world was reeling from the events of September 11th, the people of Gander did something extraordinary—they opened their homes and hearts, showing kindness and generosity when it was needed most. Together, we'll dive into stories of resilience, empathy, and the unexpected friendships that blossomed in a time of crisis. Gander’s population nearly doubled overnight, weaving a tapestry of human connection that reminds us just how much good we’re capable of—especially when the world feels darkest.
So, as we set out on this journey, let’s discover how adversity can bring out the best in us all. We’ll see how hope and unity can flourish, even in the most challenging times, and how the simple acts of everyday people can leave a lasting mark on the world.
Welcome—let’s begin this inspiring journey together.

Chapter 1: A Sudden Halt in the Skies
Picture this—a crisp September morning, where life’s routines were quietly ticking along. High above the Atlantic, hundreds of flights cut their usual paths, each one filled with people going about their lives: business travelers, families, folks chasing dreams or just heading home. Nobody knew just how quickly everything was about to change.
Suddenly, news started to ripple out—attacks in New York and Washington. All at once, the very sky people trusted became a place of uncertainty. Air traffic controllers, normally so calm and collected, were suddenly thrust into chaos, forced to make split-second decisions that would affect thousands.
Now, let’s zoom in on a small town you might never have heard of: Gander, Newfoundland. That morning started out like any other. Gander’s airport, once a key pit stop for crossing the Atlantic, had settled into a slower pace over the years. Locals barely noticed the planes overhead anymore. But that day, something felt off. The airport staff started getting message after message from air traffic control—each one more urgent than the last.
In just minutes, airspace across North America began to close. Flights were being rerouted, and Gander’s quiet airport was suddenly front and center. Imagine this—Gander was home to around 10,000 people, but almost 7,000 unexpected guests were about to land, each one with their own fears and hopes, just looking for a safe place to be.
When the first planes touched down, it was clear: this was no ordinary day. Jets from all over the world lined the runways. Most passengers had no idea what was really happening back in the United States, and landing in a remote Canadian town? It was confusing—maybe even scary. Some worried about friends and family far away. Others just wondered what would happen next. The uncertainty hung in the air.
Inside, the airport staff scrambled to figure things out—food, shelter, security—there was no playbook for an emergency like this. But as the hours ticked by, you could feel a shift. A quiet determination set in. People in Gander, and even in nearby towns, rolled up their sleeves and got ready to help in ways they’d never imagined.
Here’s something a lot of folks miss: when disaster strikes, the world tends to focus on the big cities—the places in the headlines. But in Gander, the impact was just as real, just as immediate. Many locals had never even met someone from outside Canada. Suddenly, they were asked to become hosts, stepping into a story that would push the boundaries of generosity and resilience.
As the day stretched on, the airport echoed with anxious voices. Some people tried desperately to reach loved ones. Others just sat, lost in their thoughts. And through it all, the airport crew kept moving, doing their best under impossible circumstances. For now, Gander was the safest place these travelers could possibly be.
With little warning—and almost no time to prepare—a small town in Newfoundland flung open its doors to the world, ready to care for thousands of strangers, not knowing for how long, but determined to do everything they could.

Chapter 2: Strangers Arrive, and a Community Responds
Imagine the first hours after those planes touched down—confusion and worry filling the air. Passengers, tired from their long flights, had barely any idea why they'd landed in Gander. Some guessed it was just mechanical trouble, maybe a weather delay. But bit by bit, the truth started to seep in: something terrible had happened back in the United States, and nobody was leaving anytime soon.
Now, for the people of Gander, the sudden arrival of all these unexpected guests was more than a logistical headache—it was a real test of what the community was made of. Town leaders—teachers, clergy, business owners, and volunteers—came together fast. There weren’t any grand speeches or formal sit-downs. Just a simple, shared understanding: we need to do something, and we need to do it now.
One school principal, who was used to wrangling classrooms and lesson plans, suddenly found herself sorting out sleeping spaces for hundreds of people. A bus driver who usually just shuttled local kids was now responsible for getting passengers from the airport to makeshift shelters. Churches, schools, and community centers swung their doors wide open without a moment’s hesitation.
And as the passengers stepped off those planes, they weren’t met with suspicion or fear. Instead, they were greeted with genuine warmth. Volunteers handed out sandwiches, blankets, and, maybe most importantly, a listening ear. Some travelers, still in shock, just couldn’t believe the kindness. Picture a woman from Europe, separated from her family by an ocean, finding comfort in sharing tea with a local couple. Or a businessman, used to the blur and anonymity of airports, suddenly invited into someone’s home for a hot meal.
But the generosity didn’t stop at food or shelter. Many stranded passengers were desperate for news, anxious to hear from loved ones. Gander’s phone lines, never built for this kind of surge, jammed up almost instantly. So, locals just handed over their own cell phones and home phones, inviting total strangers to call anyone they needed, for as long as it took. For some, these simple moments of connection were a lifeline—a reminder they weren’t alone.
Even the kids felt the weight of the crisis. Some were scared, not sure where they were or what would happen next. Local teachers and parents stepped up, planning games and activities to comfort and distract them. In one school gym, children from all over the world played together. Their laughter echoed—a small but powerful sign that even in tough times, life could keep moving forward.
As night fell, the town’s efforts took on a new urgency. Cots and sleeping bags filled classrooms and auditoriums. Volunteers stayed up late, making sure everyone was okay. Sure, there were moments of exhaustion and frustration. But there was also this incredible sense of shared purpose. You know, most people don’t realize how quickly a community can snap into action—until they need to. In Gander, it just happened. It was almost instinctive, a reflection of values passed quietly from one generation to the next.
By the end of that first day, something amazing was happening. Strangers were turning into neighbors, drawn together by the situation and kept afloat by kindness. The crisis wasn’t over—not by a long shot. But in Gander, a new story was being written, one not about fear or anger, but about compassion and hope.

Chapter 3: Everyday People Become Unlikely Heroes
As the days rolled by, that first wave of shock started to fade. For the passengers stranded so far from home—now affectionately called “plane people” by the locals—a new kind of routine slowly took shape. Meals were served up in the bustling school cafeterias, everyone made their beds and straightened their sleeping spaces each morning, and friendly volunteers stopped by to check what folks might need. The surreal feeling began to wear off, replaced by a steady rhythm: daily life, just under truly extraordinary circumstances.
It was in this new world that ordinary folks found themselves stepping into roles they never expected. Take the retired nurse, for example. She’d planned to spend her week out in the garden, but instead, she became the go-to medical coordinator at one of the shelters. She checked in on the elderly, handed out medication, and, maybe most importantly, offered a calming word to anyone feeling scared or sick. Her steady presence made all the difference, especially for people who felt vulnerable and so far from home.
Then there was the local baker, famous in town for his early morning deliveries. Once the crisis hit, he started baking extra loaves every night—working quietly before dawn so there’d be enough fresh bread for everyone. For many passengers, the smell of that bread in the morning was a gentle reminder of normal life, a little comfort in a world suddenly turned upside down.
Of course, it wasn’t all smooth sailing. Some passengers, frustrated by the uncertainty and desperate for news, started to feel impatient. They worried about their jobs, their families, their own safety. And in those tough moments, the volunteers met them with patience and understanding. They listened to complaints, offered whatever reassurance they could, and did their best to keep spirits up. It became clear that real kindness wasn’t just about food or shelter—it was about meeting people where they were, emotionally as well as physically.
One local family, already squeezed for space with visiting relatives, opened their home to a group of passengers who had nowhere else to go. They shuffled furniture, shared their meals, and made room for strangers in their daily routine. It wasn’t always easy—there were awkward moments and misunderstandings—but it also brought unexpected joy. Over shared dinners and late-night chats, the barriers began to fall away. Stories were swapped, friendships started to form, and soon, the line between host and guest began to blur.
For the passengers, this experience was life-changing. Many had never even heard of a place like Gander, let alone imagined they’d have to rely on the kindness of strangers. Some found themselves taking a hard look at their own lives, reevaluating what really mattered. In the middle of this crisis, all those usual markers of status and success just faded into the background. What was left? A simple truth: we’re all vulnerable sometimes, and every single person is capable of helping.
Now, the town’s response wasn’t perfect. There were days when people felt stretched thin, times when folks disagreed about how to divvy up supplies, and real anxiety about how long everything would last. But underneath it all, a spirit of generosity kept shining through. Most of us tend to think heroism is about dramatic acts or special training. But in Gander, it was clear—heroism could be as simple as showing up, lending a hand, and refusing to look away.
As the days went on, the ties between locals and passengers only grew stronger. Kids who’d arrived as total strangers now played together in the schoolyard. Adults swapped stories over coffee, discovering common ground in the most unexpected places. This crisis, for all its challenges, had brought out the very best in people, revealing strengths and kindness that might have otherwise gone unseen.

Chapter 4: Hospitality That Crosses All Boundaries
The days right after those planes landed in Gander were unlike anything the town had ever seen. People didn’t stop to ask where the passengers came from, what languages they spoke, or what they believed in. Instead, everyone just focused on what truly mattered—making sure their unexpected guests had food, shelter, comfort, and a sense of connection.
Picture this: inside one of the community centers, volunteers were busy preparing meals for folks from all over the world. The menu? Well, it was a bit of an improvisation, using whatever they could get their hands on. But every single effort was made to respect dietary needs and personal preferences. There was even a group of vegetarians from India, who at first were worried about what they’d be able to eat. To their surprise, the volunteers had cooked up a special meal just for them—after researching recipes and calling local stores for ingredients. That kind of care meant everything.
And when it came to religious differences, the same spirit of understanding shone through. Jewish passengers looking for a place to pray found the doors of a local synagogue wide open, even though the congregation itself was small. Muslim guests were given private spaces for their daily prayers, too. In every situation, the answer was simple: let’s listen, let’s learn, and let’s make room for everyone.
You can imagine how much this meant to the passengers. One man from the Middle East, who was used to being treated with suspicion in airports, found nothing but warmth and acceptance in Gander. A woman traveling on her own—who’d been feeling anxious about her safety—was completely reassured by the kindness around her. In a world that so often feels divided by fear and mistrust, Gander’s response was a powerful reminder that real hospitality knows no boundaries.
And it didn’t stop at the basics. Local businesses stepped up, donating clothes, toiletries, and other essentials. Pharmacies filled prescriptions for free. Hairdressers gave complimentary haircuts, and musicians put together impromptu concerts to lift everyone’s spirits. The town’s radio station became a lifeline, sharing updates and letting passengers send messages out to their families across the globe.
There were even moments of celebration. Birthdays were marked with cakes and songs, anniversaries with small gatherings and thoughtful gifts. In one shelter, a couple who had planned to get married in the United States decided, why not get married right here in Gander? The whole community pitched in—flowers, music, even a wedding cake. That simple ceremony turned into a symbol of hope, proof that life could go on, even in the shadow of tragedy.
In the end, the experience changed everyone—hosts and guests alike. For the people of Gander, it was a chance to live out the values they’d always believed in: kindness, generosity, and the power of community. And for the passengers, it was a lesson in trust—a reminder that help can show up when you least expect it, and from people you’ve never met before.
As the days passed, the initial sense of crisis faded, replaced by something much deeper—a lasting connection. Many passengers promised to come back some day, to keep in touch, and to always remember the kindness they’d received. And for Gander, these memories became a source of pride, a story to pass down to future generations.

Chapter 5: Facing Uncertainty Together
As the days in Gander stretched on, the outside world felt both distant and painfully real. News of the attacks in the United States trickled in—sometimes through TVs set up in community halls, other times in hushed conversations between passengers. The shock, the grief, you could feel it in the air. But there was also this unmistakable determination—people wanted to keep moving forward, somehow.
If you ask anyone who was there, they’ll tell you: the hardest part was the not knowing. When would the planes be allowed to leave? What would they return to back home? Some folks worried about their jobs, their families, or even their own safety. Others found themselves struggling with helplessness, realizing there was nothing to do but wait—and hope.
That’s when the community’s support became more important than ever. Volunteers checked in regularly, offering a kind word or just listening. Local counselors and clergy stepped up, comforting those who were grieving or anxious. In one of the shelters, passengers started gathering every evening just to share stories—finding comfort in the simple act of being together.
Of course, it wasn’t always easy. Supplies ran low now and then, and sometimes tempers flared. People disagreed about how to share resources, and even the most dedicated volunteers felt the pressure. But you know what? Through all the challenges, a sense of shared purpose kept everyone going.
Most people don’t realize just how much strength a community can have until it’s put to the test. In Gander, the crisis uncovered a resilience that surprised even the locals. People who’d never met before rolled up their sleeves and worked together—solving problems, supporting each other. The lines between host and guest, local and visitor, started to fade away.
As the days passed, the thought of leaving became real. Passengers packed up, exchanged phone numbers and email addresses, and said their goodbyes. There were hugs, tears, and promises that this connection wouldn’t just disappear. For so many, these days had changed their lives—a powerful reminder of what kindness can do, and how important it is to reach out when things get tough.
The people of Gander were changed, too. The crisis had pushed them to their limits, but it also reaffirmed what they valued most. When faced with uncertainty, they chose to respond with compassion, not fear—with generosity, not self-interest. The story of those days became a part of the town’s identity—a living example of what’s possible when ordinary people come together during extraordinary times.

Chapter 6. The Long Wait and the Weight of News.
There’s a certain kind of limbo that settles in when you’re far from home—stuck, unable to move forward, and not really sure what’s coming next.
For the passengers stranded in Gander, those days right after September 11th seemed to stretch on forever, weighed down by a heavy uncertainty.
Every morning, people woke up in borrowed beds, surrounded by faces they’d never seen before, and wondered, “Will today finally be the day we get to leave?”
News from the outside world came slowly—sometimes just a whisper, other times like a tidal wave.
In school gyms and church basements, people would huddle around TVs, watching the same scenes play over and over: smoke rising, sirens blaring, faces streaked with tears.
Some people learned that friends or coworkers had been lost in the attacks. Others spent hours waiting, dialing and redialing phone numbers, just hoping to hear a loved one’s voice on the other end.
I remember one man—a father, there for work—who sat by the phone for hours, his hands shaking as he tried again and again to reach his family in New York.
Every failed call seemed to make his worry heavier. But you know what? A local volunteer sat beside him, offering quiet company and a hot cup of tea. In those moments, the kindness of a stranger felt like a lifeline.
And it wasn’t just the passengers who felt the strain—the volunteers did, too. Many had their own families and jobs, but they kept coming back, serving meals, organizing supplies, and just being there for anyone who needed a shoulder.
There were moments when exhaustion threatened to knock them down, but the simple gratitude from the passengers kept them going. It was clear that, in a crisis, sometimes the smallest gestures carry the greatest weight.
As the days passed, a bit of routine started to settle in. Meals were served at the same times, and volunteers would check on the shelters each morning.
Kids went back to their lessons—sometimes with new friends from halfway across the world. The town’s radio station became a comfort, sharing news and playing music that reminded everyone of home.
Most people don’t realize just how much strength it takes to wait—to hold on to hope when the future feels so uncertain.
In Gander, this long wait became a real test of patience and resilience. It was a reminder that sometimes, when you can’t do anything else, the best thing is to stand together and face the unknown—side by side.

Bonds Forged in Shared Experience
As the days in Gander stretched on, something truly amazing started to unfold. That awkwardness—the hesitation you might feel as a stranger in a new place—began to melt away. Instead, people who’d never met before found themselves sharing dinners, swapping stories, and laughing together. It’s like the crisis stripped away all the usual walls we put up, leaving behind just one simple truth: we’re all in this together.
Picture this: in one shelter, passengers from all over the world would gather each night to cook meals from their own countries. The kitchen would fill with the warm aroma of spices, fresh bread baking, and a lively blend of conversations in different languages. One local woman, curious about these new and unfamiliar dishes, decided to join in. Pretty soon, she was picking up new recipes and making friends over a simmering pot. Cooking together became more than just making dinner—it was a chance to bridge cultures, to find real connection even when everything else felt uncertain.
There were moments of celebration, too. When a child’s birthday rolled around, volunteers put together a party, complete with cake and a handful of balloons. Kids from all over—some hardly speaking a word of English—joined in the singing and games. And just for a little while, all those worries and fears faded out, replaced by the pure joy of simply being together.
Some of the connections ran even deeper. One passenger, grieving the loss of a loved one in the attacks, found comfort in the friendship of a local couple. They’d spend long evenings talking, sharing memories, and quietly hoping for better days ahead. That kindness—those gentle conversations—helped the traveler start to heal, little by little.
What became clear was this: the crisis had created a kind of family. Not one tied by blood, but by everything they’d been through together. Many passengers made promises to return to Gander someday, or to stay in touch with the people who had cared for them during those uncertain hours. And for the locals, those friendships became a point of pride, and a lasting comfort—a living reminder that, even in the darkest times, real connection is possible.
Most of us never expect to meet lifelong friends in the middle of a crisis, right? But in Gander, the bonds forged during those incredible days would last long after the planes took off and the world moved on.

Chapter Eight: The Departure—Bittersweet Goodbyes.
When word finally spread that the planes could take off, you could almost feel the shift in the air around Gander. There was relief, sure—but also a kind of quiet sadness. Passengers started packing up, getting ready to leave the little town that had become a safe haven for nearly a week. Gander was about to settle back into its usual routine, but you just knew the memories would stick around for a long, long time.
The departures didn’t all happen at once. Instead, groups of passengers were called to the airport bit by bit. Local volunteers were everywhere—helping with luggage, handing out snacks for the road, and even slipping handwritten notes with phone numbers and addresses into people’s hands. There were hugs. There were tears. And there were so many heartfelt promises to keep in touch. For a lot of folks, heading home felt both wonderful and a little heartbreaking. They were grateful to be going back, but saying goodbye to new friends was tougher than they expected.
Take one woman, for example. She’d arrived in Gander scared and completely lost. By the end, she found herself crying as she hugged her hosts goodbye—pressing a scarf, something she’d carried from home, into their hands to say thank you. The family promised to write, and as she boarded the bus to the airport, she glanced back through the window, waving one more time.
At the airport, the emotions ran high. Passengers and volunteers swapped stories and contact details, snapping quick photos so they wouldn’t forget these moments. Out by the runway, some locals stood quietly, waving as the planes lifted off—proud, but just a little sad to see this chapter close.
For Gander, the departure of the “plane people” really did mark the end of something extraordinary. The town slipped back to its slower pace, but everyone knew things had changed. The generosity and kindness shown in those days became something to talk about, to pass down to future generations—a story of hope right when it was needed most.
Here’s the thing: most people don’t realize just how tough it is to say goodbye to someone you’ve helped through a crisis. In Gander, those farewells spoke volumes about the connections formed in just a few days. It’s a powerful reminder that even the briefest encounters can change lives in ways you’d never expect.

Chapter 9: Ripples Across the World
Even after all the planes had taken off, the story of Gander’s incredible hospitality just kept traveling. Passengers went home and started telling everyone they knew—friends, family, even total strangers—about the warmth and generosity they’d found in this little Canadian town.
Letters and emails started pouring in from all over, filled with gratitude and admiration for the people of Gander. It was as if the kindness they’d experienced there couldn’t help but spill out into the world.
Some of those passengers wanted to do more, so they organized fundraisers to support Gander’s schools and community centers—hoping to give back, even just a little. Others made trips back, bringing their families to meet the folks who had cared for them during those uncertain days. The connections formed in Gander didn’t just fade away; they grew into new friendships, partnerships, and even a few marriages.
Word kept spreading, far beyond Newfoundland. News outlets across the globe picked up the story, shining a spotlight on the town’s response and showing just how powerful simple kindness can be, especially in the face of tragedy. For so many, Gander became a symbol of hope—a reminder that, even when things are at their darkest, ordinary people can make an extraordinary difference.
One passenger, fueled by her experience, started a community project back home, encouraging her neighbors to look out for each other when times got tough. Another, a teacher, brought Gander’s story into her classroom, using it as a lesson in empathy and compassion for her students. You could see the ripples of Gander’s kindness spreading outward, touching lives in ways no one could’ve imagined.
For the people of Gander, all this recognition was both humbling and a little overwhelming. They never set out to be heroes—they just did what felt right. But the impact of their actions couldn’t be denied. It was a powerful reminder of what community can do, and how lasting generosity really is.
Most people don’t realize just how far a single act of kindness can reach. In Gander, the effects went around the world—a beautiful reminder that compassion doesn’t care about borders.

Chapter 10: Lessons That Endure
Even years after September 2001, Gander’s story still holds a special place in the hearts of those who lived through it. You might’ve seen it celebrated in books, documentaries, maybe even heard about that Broadway musical. But for the folks who were actually there, the real legacy? Well, it’s a lot quieter, and way more personal.
The experience changed the way so many locals saw themselves—and their town. Suddenly, it was clear: when life throws something big your way, you don’t need grand gestures. It’s those small, everyday acts of kindness, repeated over and over, that really make a difference. The crisis didn’t give them new strengths; it just brought out the ones that had always been there, waiting for the right moment.
For the passengers who landed in Gander, the kindness they found still feels fresh. Many have kept in touch with their hosts, swapping letters, emails, even holiday cards. Some folks have even come back to visit—bringing their kids along to meet the people who once opened their homes and hearts. Those connections, built in just a few days, have lasted for years. Isn’t that something? It really shows you how powerful simple human connection can be.
But here’s what sticks with me: the story of Gander isn’t just about what happened that September. It’s about the choices we all make—every single day. Choices to help, to listen, to open our doors when someone needs it most. It’s a gentle reminder that, even in a world that sometimes feels divided or uncertain, there’s always space for kindness.
And honestly, most people don’t realize just how much one community can do. Gander makes it clear: when people come together, amazing things can happen.

As we wrap up, let's take a moment to sit with what really matters here. Little acts of kindness—they have this amazing way of reaching further than we ever expect. Real community? It’s not about dramatic gestures or headlines. It’s built, day by day, through simple generosity and genuine care. When life throws us into crisis, it’s often the everyday folks who become unexpected beacons of hope. And true hospitality? It’s about meeting people right where they are—without judgment, and without fear. The connections we make in tough times—they tend to last, quietly shaping our lives long after the moment has passed.
The story of Gander really brings all of this to life. Even when the world seemed to be falling apart, a small town stepped up, opening its doors and hearts to total strangers. Nobody waited to be told what to do, or looked for praise. They just acted—with empathy, with courage, and with a deep sense of looking out for one another. So, if you ever wonder whether your own actions matter, think back to Gander. Every little gesture of kindness, no matter how small, can help someone feel seen, safe, and valued. And in a world that can feel divided, the lessons from Gander invite us to reach out, to listen, and to care just a little more. Next time you’re faced with a choice—to help, to welcome, or to simply stand by—let the spirit of Gander nudge you forward. Because you never know whose life you might touch, or just how far your kindness will travel.
